items.stem: Which term matches this description: "The ability of a country to produce a good at a lower opportunity cost than another country"?
items.answer: comparative advantage
items.markingKey: B. This is the definition of comparative advantage.

items.stem: "Comparative advantage means that everybody in a country gains from free trade." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: The country gains overall, but workers and firms in import-competing industries may lose; gains are not automatically shared.
items.markingKey: The country gains overall, but workers and firms in import-competing industries may lose; gains are not automatically shared. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: With the help of a specific example, explain why comparative advantage can change over time.
items.answer: Investment in human and physical capital, technology and changes in factor prices alter opportunity costs; e.g. South Korea moved from textiles to semiconductors. (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.)
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Investment in human and physical capital, technology and changes in factor prices alter opportunity costs; e.g. South Korea moved from textiles to semiconductors. items.stem: With the help of a labelled diagram, outline how two countries gain from specialisation and trade according to comparative advantage, using PPCs.
items.answer: Two straight-line PPCs with different slopes (opportunity costs); each country specialises in the good with lower opportunity cost; trade at terms between the two OCs allows consumption outside each PPC.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: Two straight-line PPCs with different slopes (opportunity costs); each country specialises in the good with lower opportunity cost; trade at terms between the two OCs allows consumption outside each PPC. items.stem: Analyse one strength and one limitation of the view that the theory of comparative advantage provides a convincing case for free trade.
items.answer: It provides a strong theoretical case, but real-world assumptions do not hold fully, so trade gains must be combined with adjustment policies.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: specialisation raises world output and consumption; lower prices and more choice; competition raises efficiency. Arguments against: assumes full employment and mobile factors; ignores transport costs and economies of scale; gains unevenly distributed; may lock developing countries into primary products. Supported judgement: It provides a strong theoretical case, but real-world assumptions do not hold fully, so trade gains must be combined with adjustment policies.

items.stem: With the same quantity of resources, Tarsia can produce 19 units of bananas or 8 units of smartphones, while Zedland can produce 9 units of bananas or 14 units of smartphones. Identify which country has the absolute advantage in bananas and calculate the opportunity cost of one unit of bananas in each country.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "trade liberalisation"?
options: The WTO process for resolving trade disagreements between members through panels and the Appellate Body
The reduction or removal of barriers to international trade
The argument for protecting strategic industries such as defence, energy, food and semiconductors to avoid dependence on other countries
The concentration of a country's resources on producing the goods in which it has a comparative advantage
items.answer: The reduction or removal of barriers to international trade
items.markingKey: B. "trade liberalisation" is the reduction or removal of barriers to international trade.

items.stem: "The WTO forces all countries to have zero tariffs." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Members negotiate bound maximum tariff rates; tariffs can remain positive, and developing countries have special and differential treatment.
items.markingKey: Members negotiate bound maximum tariff rates; tariffs can remain positive, and developing countries have special and differential treatment. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain the difference between a regional trade agreement and the WTO.
items.answer: The WTO sets multilateral rules for all 166 members on a non-discriminatory (MFN) basis; a regional trade agreement liberalises trade only among its members, discriminating against non-members.
items.markingKey: The WTO sets multilateral rules for all 166 members on a non-discriminatory (MFN) basis; a regional trade agreement liberalises trade only among its members, discriminating against non-members. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: A small country removes a 20% tariff on imported clothing after joining the WTO. Identify two groups that gain and one group that loses, explaining each.
items.answer: Gainers: consumers (lower prices, more choice); firms using imported inputs; exporters (lower costs, possible reciprocal access). Losers: domestic clothing producers and their workers, who face more competition.
items.markingKey: Gainers: consumers (lower prices, more choice); firms using imported inputs; exporters (lower costs, possible reciprocal access). Losers: domestic clothing producers and their workers, who face more competition.

items.stem: With reference to the WTO Trade Facilitation Agreement, explain how it illustrates the case for free trade.
items.answer: The WTO Trade Facilitation Agreement entered into force in 2017 to simplify customs procedures; the WTO estimated it could cut trade costs by about 14% on average. Reducing administrative barriers lowers trade costs, especially for developing countries
items.markingKey: Context (The WTO Trade Facilitation Agreement entered into force in 2017 to simplify customs procedures; the WTO estimated it could cut trade costs by about 14% on average.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Reducing administrative barriers lowers trade costs, especially for developing countries – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to the case for free trade.

items.stem: Outline two points that could be used to evaluate the claim: "The WTO has been successful in promoting free trade."
items.answer: The WTO was successful in reducing tariffs historically, but its effectiveness has weakened as major economies turn to unilateral measures and regional deals.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: average tariffs have fallen greatly since 1947; rules-based system and dispute settlement; membership of 166 countries. Arguments against: Doha Round stalled; Appellate Body paralysed since 2019; rise of US-China tariffs and industrial subsidies; agriculture remains highly protected. Supported judgement: The WTO was successful in reducing tariffs historically, but its effectiveness has weakened as major economies turn to unilateral measures and regional deals.

items.stem: Which of the following is an objective of the WTO?
options: Lending to countries with BoP problems
Reducing barriers to trade and settling trade disputes
items.answer: Reducing barriers to trade and settling trade disputes
items.markingKey: C. Lending is the IMF's role.

items.stem: Explain why developing countries have criticised the WTO.
items.answer: High-income countries maintain agricultural subsidies and tariffs on processed goods while pressing developing countries to open markets; negotiation capacity is unequal.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "production subsidy"?
options: The argument for protecting strategic industries such as defence, energy, food and semiconductors to avoid dependence on other countries
The rate at which one good is exchanged for another in international trade
The value of the next best alternative forgone when a choice is made
A payment by the government to domestic producers, lowering their costs so they can compete with imports
items.answer: A payment by the government to domestic producers, lowering their costs so they can compete with imports
items.markingKey: D. "production subsidy" is a payment by the government to domestic producers, lowering their costs so they can compete with imports.

items.stem: Explain why administrative barriers can be as restrictive as tariffs.
items.answer: Long customs procedures, unusual standards and licensing raise the cost and uncertainty of importing, reducing trade without collecting revenue.

items.stem: Halvania is a small importer of cars. Domestic demand: Qd = 143 − 2P; domestic supply: Qs = P; world price $12; proposed tariff $4 per unit (Q in thousands). Calculate the quantity of imports before and after the tariff, and the government's tariff revenue.
items.answer: Before: Qd = 119, Qs = 12, imports = 107 thousand. After (P = $16): Qd = 111, Qs = 16, imports = 95 thousand. Revenue = $4 × 95 thousand = $380 thousand.
items.markingKey: At $12: imports 119 − 12 = 107; at $16: 111 − 16 = 95; revenue = 4 × 95 = 380. [M1] for correct method/working; [A1] for imports and revenue. Award [A1] only with correct units/notation where relevant.

items.stem: "A tariff is paid by foreign exporters, so it does not harm domestic consumers." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: The tariff is paid by importers and largely passed on in higher prices; studies of the 2018 US tariffs found almost full pass-through to US prices.
items.markingKey: The tariff is paid by importers and largely passed on in higher prices; studies of the 2018 US tariffs found almost full pass-through to US prices. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Briefly describe US-China tariffs from 2018 and explain what it reveals about tariffs and retaliation.
items.answer: The USA imposed tariffs on about $370 bn of Chinese goods in 2018-2019 and China retaliated against US exports such as soybeans. Tariffs raised costs for US importers and consumers while retaliation hurt US farmers, requiring government support payments
items.markingKey: Context (The USA imposed tariffs on about $370 bn of Chinese goods in 2018-2019 and China retaliated against US exports such as soybeans.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. items.stem: Give one argument for and one argument against the view that tariffs are an effective way to protect domestic jobs.
items.answer: Tariffs may save some jobs in the protected industry but often cost more jobs elsewhere; adjustment assistance is usually more efficient.

Supported judgement: Tariffs may save some jobs in the protected industry but often cost more jobs elsewhere; adjustment assistance is usually more efficient.

items.stem: Explain why a tariff creates a welfare loss.
items.answer: Higher-cost domestic producers replace cheaper imports (production inefficiency) and consumers who valued the good above the world price no longer buy it (consumption loss); these surplus losses are not gained by anyone.

items.stem: Explain the difference between an import quota and a tariff.
items.answer: A tariff raises the price of imports and generates government revenue, but the quantity of imports can vary; a quota fixes the quantity of imports, and the extra revenue goes to licence holders rather than the government.
items.markingKey: A tariff raises the price of imports and generates government revenue, but the quantity of imports can vary; a quota fixes the quantity of imports, and the extra revenue goes to licence holders rather than the government. items.stem: Isabel writes: "A country with no absolute advantage in anything cannot gain from trade." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: It still has a comparative advantage in the good where its relative disadvantage is smallest (lowest OC), and both countries gain by specialising accordingly.
items.markingKey: It still has a comparative advantage in the good where its relative disadvantage is smallest (lowest OC), and both countries gain by specialising accordingly. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Draw a diagram to illustrate the effects of a tariff on a small importing economy, and outline what it shows.
items.answer: Domestic D and S with world price Pw (horizontal world supply); tariff raises price to Pw + t; domestic output rises, consumption falls, imports fall; label consumer surplus loss, producer surplus gain, government revenue and the two welfare-loss triangles.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: Domestic D and S with world price Pw (horizontal world supply); tariff raises price to Pw + t; domestic output rises, consumption falls, imports fall; label consumer surplus loss, producer surplus gain, government revenue and the two welfare-loss triangles. Award up to 2 marks for an accurate, fully labelled diagram and up to 4 for the explanation linked to it.

items.stem: Briefly describe the US-EU Airbus-Boeing dispute and explain what it reveals about the role of the WTO.
items.answer: The WTO ruled that both the EU and the USA had given illegal subsidies to aircraft makers, authorising tariffs; the two sides agreed a five-year truce in 2021. Dispute settlement provided legal rulings and authorised retaliation, encouraging a negotiated settlement
items.markingKey: Context (The WTO ruled that both the EU and the USA had given illegal subsidies to aircraft makers, authorising tariffs; the two sides agreed a five-year truce in 2021.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Dispute settlement provided legal rulings and authorised retaliation, encouraging a negotiated settlement – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to the role of the WTO.

items.stem: With reference to EU anti-dumping duties on Chinese solar panels, explain how it illustrates anti-dumping as an argument for protection.
items.answer: In 2013 the EU imposed anti-dumping duties on Chinese solar panels, later replaced by minimum import prices until 2018. Protecting EU producers from below-cost imports raised the cost of solar installations for European consumers
items.markingKey: Context (In 2013 the EU imposed anti-dumping duties on Chinese solar panels, later replaced by minimum import prices until 2018.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Protecting EU producers from below-cost imports raised the cost of solar installations for European consumers – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to anti-dumping as an argument for protection.

items.stem: Outline two points that could be used to evaluate the claim: "The theory of comparative advantage provides a convincing case for free trade."
items.answer: It provides a strong theoretical case, but real-world assumptions do not hold fully, so trade gains must be combined with adjustment policies.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: specialisation raises world output and consumption; lower prices and more choice; competition raises efficiency. Arguments against: assumes full employment and mobile factors; ignores transport costs and economies of scale; gains unevenly distributed; may lock developing countries into primary products. Supported judgement: It provides a strong theoretical case, but real-world assumptions do not hold fully, so trade gains must be combined with adjustment policies.

items.stem:
Read the extract below.

After the USA imposed safeguard tariffs on washing machines in 2018, their prices rose by about 12%, and the prices of dryers (not subject to tariffs) also rose.

Using information from the extract and your knowledge of economics, evaluate the view that tariffs are an effective way to protect domestic jobs.
items.answer: Tariffs may save some jobs in the protected industry but often cost more jobs elsewhere; adjustment assistance is usually more efficient.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: protect jobs in import-competing industries in the short run; raise government revenue; can buy time for adjustment. Arguments against: jobs lost in user industries and exporters hit by retaliation; high cost per job saved; consumers pay higher prices; reduce incentives to become efficient. Judgement: Tariffs may save some jobs in the protected industry but often cost more jobs elsewhere; adjustment assistance is usually more efficient. Reward explicit use of the extract. items.stem: Evaluate the claim that the WTO has been successful in promoting free trade.
items.answer: The WTO was successful in reducing tariffs historically, but its effectiveness has weakened as major economies turn to unilateral measures and regional deals.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: average tariffs have fallen greatly since 1947; rules-based system and dispute settlement; membership of 166 countries. Arguments against: Doha Round stalled; Appellate Body paralysed since 2019; rise of US-China tariffs and industrial subsidies; agriculture remains highly protected. Supported judgement: The WTO was successful in reducing tariffs historically, but its effectiveness has weakened as major economies turn to unilateral measures and regional deals. items.stem:
Read the extract below.

In April 2025 the US government announced a baseline 10% tariff on most imports, with higher rates for many countries, citing trade deficits and national security.

In 2013 the EU imposed anti-dumping duties on Chinese solar panels, later replaced by minimum import prices until 2018.

Using information from the extract and your knowledge of economics, evaluate the view that the arguments for trade protection outweigh the arguments against it.
items.answer: Most economists conclude that the costs of protection usually outweigh its benefits, except for narrow cases such as genuine dumping or strategic security concerns.

items.stem: Which of the following is a source of comparative advantage?
options: Differences in factor endowments such as land, labour and capital
items.answer: Differences in factor endowments such as land, labour and capital
items.markingKey: D. Heckscher-Ohlin explanation.

items.stem: Outline the meaning of the term "import quota".
items.answer: A legal limit on the quantity or value of a good that can be imported
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: a legal limit on the quantity or value of a good that can be imported. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "dispute settlement"?
options: International trade without government-imposed barriers such as tariffs, quotas and subsidies
The ability of a country to produce a good at a lower opportunity cost than another country
Non-tariff barriers such as complex customs procedures, strict standards, licensing and health and safety regulations that make importing more difficult
The WTO process for resolving trade disagreements between members through panels and the Appellate Body
items.answer: The WTO process for resolving trade disagreements between members through panels and the Appellate Body
items.markingKey: D. "dispute settlement" is the WTO process for resolving trade disagreements between members through panels and the Appellate Body.

items.stem: Explain the difference between arguments against trade protection and arguments for trade protection.
items.answer: For: protecting infant industries, jobs, national security, anti-dumping, raising revenue, correcting BoP deficits. Against: higher prices, inefficiency, misallocation of resources, retaliation and reduced export competitiveness.
items.markingKey: For: protecting infant industries, jobs, national security, anti-dumping, raising revenue, correcting BoP deficits. Against: higher prices, inefficiency, misallocation of resources, retaliation and reduced export competitiveness. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain why both countries can gain from trade even if one has an absolute advantage in both goods.
items.answer: Opportunity costs differ; if each specialises in the good with lower OC and they trade at terms between their OCs, each obtains the other good more cheaply than producing it, so total output and consumption rise.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Opportunity costs differ; if each specialises in the good with lower OC and they trade at terms between their OCs, each obtains the other good more cheaply than producing it, so total output and consumption rise. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Briefly explain why a tariff may harm domestic firms that use the protected good as an input.
items.answer: They must pay a higher price for the input, raising costs, reducing competitiveness and possibly employment in user industries (e.g. US car makers after steel tariffs).
items.markingKey: Award marks for: They must pay a higher price for the input, raising costs, reducing competitiveness and possibly employment in user industries (e.g. US car makers after steel tariffs). (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Distinguish between the WTO and a regional trade agreement.
items.answer: The WTO sets multilateral rules for all 166 members on a non-discriminatory (MFN) basis; a regional trade agreement liberalises trade only among its members, discriminating against non-members.
items.markingKey: The WTO sets multilateral rules for all 166 members on a non-discriminatory (MFN) basis; a regional trade agreement liberalises trade only among its members, discriminating against non-members. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain why protection may lead to inefficiency in domestic industries.
items.answer: Protected firms face less competition, so they have weaker incentives to cut costs and innovate, resulting in productive and dynamic inefficiency.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Protected firms face less competition, so they have weaker incentives to cut costs and innovate, resulting in productive and dynamic inefficiency. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Felix writes: "Comparative advantage means that everybody in a country gains from free trade." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: The country gains overall, but workers and firms in import-competing industries may lose; gains are not automatically shared.
items.markingKey: The country gains overall, but workers and firms in import-competing industries may lose; gains are not automatically shared. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Using US-China tariffs from 2018 as an example, explain tariffs and retaliation.
items.answer: The USA imposed tariffs on about $370 bn of Chinese goods in 2018-2019 and China retaliated against US exports such as soybeans. Tariffs raised costs for US importers and consumers while retaliation hurt US farmers, requiring government support payments
items.markingKey: Context (The USA imposed tariffs on about $370 bn of Chinese goods in 2018-2019 and China retaliated against US exports such as soybeans.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Tariffs raised costs for US importers and consumers while retaliation hurt US farmers, requiring government support payments – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to tariffs and retaliation.

items.stem: Outline one way in which the WTO Trade Facilitation Agreement shows the case for free trade.
items.answer: The WTO Trade Facilitation Agreement entered into force in 2017 to simplify customs procedures; the WTO estimated it could cut trade costs by about 14% on average. Reducing administrative barriers lowers trade costs, especially for developing countries
items.markingKey: Context (The WTO Trade Facilitation Agreement entered into force in 2017 to simplify customs procedures; the WTO estimated it could cut trade costs by about 14% on average.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Reducing administrative barriers lowers trade costs, especially for developing countries – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to the case for free trade.

items.stem: With reference to South Korea's use of infant industry protection, explain how it illustrates the infant industry argument.
items.answer: South Korea protected and subsidised industries such as steel, shipbuilding and cars in the 1960s-1980s while requiring firms to export. Temporary protection combined with export targets helped firms like Hyundai and POSCO become globally competitive
items.markingKey: Context (South Korea protected and subsidised industries such as steel, shipbuilding and cars in the 1960s-1980s while requiring firms to export.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Temporary protection combined with export targets helped firms like Hyundai and POSCO become globally competitive – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to the infant industry argument.

items.stem: With reference to Taiwan's semiconductor industry, explain how it illustrates how comparative advantage can be created.
items.answer: TSMC in Taiwan produces over 90% of the world's most advanced chips. Decades of investment in skills, R&D and capital created a comparative advantage in high-tech manufacturing
items.markingKey: Context (TSMC in Taiwan produces over 90% of the world's most advanced chips.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Decades of investment in skills, R&D and capital created a comparative advantage in high-tech manufacturing – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to how comparative advantage can be created.

items.stem: Country A: 1 worker produces 6 tonnes of rice or 3 machines. Country B: 1 worker produces 4 tonnes of rice or 4 machines. Show that both countries gain if A specialises in rice and B in machines and they trade at 1 machine = 1.5 tonnes of rice.
items.answer: OC of 1 machine: A 2 rice, B 1 rice. B has comparative advantage in machines, A in rice. At ToT 1.5 rice per machine: A pays 1.5 rice instead of 2; B gets 1.5 rice instead of 1. Both gain.
items.markingKey: OC of 1 machine: A 2 rice, B 1 rice. B has comparative advantage in machines, A in rice. At ToT 1.5 rice per machine: A pays 1.5 rice instead of 2; B gets 1.5 rice instead of 1. Both gain.
